papers.title: Chimera states in a network of firefly oscillators
papers.abstract: We investigate chimera-like states in a network of identical firefly oscillators with nonlocal delayed coupling. For a uniform communication delay, the network exhibits a breathing phase-frequency chimera, characterized by the coexistence of frequency-locked and frequency-drifting populations and an oscillating incoherent-domain width. We then introduce heterogeneous pairwise communication delays to investigate a numerical analogue of the Sarfati-Peleg phenomenon observed in natural firefly swarms. In this regime, a recurring collective chorus coexists with character oscillators that flash persistently before or after the chorus. Cycle-resolved delay maps, role rasters, character probabilities, and spatial covariance diagnostics demonstrate the persistence and collective organization of these chorus-character roles. Although the uniform-delay and heterogeneous-delay states represent different forms of partial synchronization, the same firefly-oscillator framework supports both regimes. Finally, we construct a reduced analytical description in terms of a chorus-relative delay field and a memory field. The local dynamics is organized around a saturated subcritical pitchfork structure, producing a stable chorus equilibrium together with two stable character equilibria. The reduced model therefore provides a phenomenological description of the tri-stable chorus-character organization and its characteristic delay scale. Our results show that heterogeneous delayed interactions among identical relaxation oscillators can generate persistent temporal identities analogous to those reported in synchronous firefly swarms.

papers.title: Learning memory forces and bounding frequency errors in fractional Kuramoto grids
papers.abstract: Missing history creates two different demands on a forecaster for a fractional grid: predicting frequency accurately and reconstructing memory well enough to bound the prediction error. We connect these demands through the hereditary force that remains after an integral observation correction. A compact decoder retains the directions most relevant to that force, and an exact decomposition separates omitted directions from coefficient error. A response-trained linear predictor and neural refinement learn the coefficients for frequency prediction. A separate force reconstruction supplies the reference for a nonlinear energy bound for the specified finite relaxation model, accounting for numerical propagation defects and the difference between the reference and point forecasts. For the outage transients studied here, refinement improves on the linear predictor across the time steps and memory parameters tested. Replacing the noisy origin states reveals why this gain can coexist with greater memory reconstruction error: the learned correction partly compensates for observation error. Separating prediction from reconstruction enables frequency bounds in cases where the point predictor alone cannot support them. A critical radius compares calibrated uncertainty with the angle margin available along the reference trajectory, explaining both issuance and abstention. Under jointly exchangeable calibration and test events, the calibrated guarantee bounds the marginal probability of issuing an invalid envelope. Together, these results connect uncertainty about history outside the observation window to frequency forecasts and explicit conditions for bounding their errors.

papers.title: Data-driven Reconstruction of the Phase Dynamics for the El Niño-Southern Oscillation Reveals Seasonality and Statistical Synchronization with the Annual Cycle
papers.abstract: In this study, we treat the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) as a rhythmic system periodically forced by the annual cycle. We examine ENSO event seasonality and synchronization between the annual and ENSO cycles. We compute phase time series for both cycles from sea surface temperature data using a data-driven Koopman operator approach. We then use Bayesian inference to reconstruct phase equations describing how the phases of the two oscillators evolve. The reconstructed two-variable phase equations show that the annual cycle modulates the instantaneous frequency of the fundamental ENSO mode. Stochastic simulations of these equations incorporating the estimated stationary noise indicate that El Ni\~{n}o and La Ni\~{n}a events tend to last longer when they start in boreal summer and that the variability of their durations is greater when they start in boreal spring. Furthermore, the averaged form of the phase equations indicates statistical $3:1$ phase locking between the annual and ENSO cycles, whereas no statistical phase locking is found for the other $m:n$ ratios.

papers.title: Cup and cap synchronization: higher-order node dynamics from topology
papers.abstract: Higher-order node-based synchronization provides distinct mechanisms for discontinuous synchronization transitions. However, a comprehensive theoretical framework capable of encompassing existing models and revealing the role of higher-order interactions beyond triangles is still missing. Here, combining algebraic topology and nonlinear dynamics, we introduce Cup and Cap Synchronization, a unifying theoretical framework for higher-order node-based dynamics that naturally incorporates the topological organization of the underlying higher-order network. We show that Cup and Cap Synchronization can display critical behavior belonging to the universality classes of two existing higher-order Kuramoto-like models, whose distinct critical behaviors were thought to originate from different mechanisms. Remarkably, we demonstrate that Cup and Cap Synchronization displays additional phenomenology not captured by the previously proposed models of higher-order node-based synchronization. Most relevantly, the inclusion of four-body interactions can fundamentally alter the critical properties of the synchronization transition, giving rise to collective phenomena that cannot be observed in models including only interactions mediated by edges and triangles. These findings reveal the importance of going beyond the commonly studied three-body terms and establish Cup and Cap Synchronization as a unifying theoretical framework for understanding collective dynamics in higher-order networks.
